speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I mentioned earlier the comments that the hon. gentleman had made and referred to his suggestion that Canada, in this case the supplier, should have sole ownership and control of the spent fuel, or the fuel rods, or whatever the technical expression is. We are presently negotiating to have included within our bilateral agreements a veto of control over the use of any spent fuel. We think that is an extremely important item in the agreement and we are working in that direction. It is not precisely the same idea as the hon. member's, but I think it has the same effect. If that can be achieved-and it is certainly our objective-we hope to do this not only bilaterally but multilaterally among other exporters.
I wanted to say a word about a number of the matters the hon. member for Greenwood and others raised, especially his reference to international economic development.
I think it would be unfortunate in this particular year if we failed to refer, at least in some brief words, to this whole question of international development. It is certainly a matter of gratification to me that all members of the House are now extending their interest in international development beyond the operations of the Canadian International Development Agency to cover some of the wider policy issues now under consideration throughout the world.
As hon. members may be aware, the government of Canada has undertaken, through an interdepartmental committee under the chairmanship of the undersecretary of state for external affairs, a comprehensive study of the economic relations between the developing and the developed world. I think it is a good thing that the House approved today the reference inviting the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence to examine the whole field of policy relating to international development, but particularly to focus attention upon economic relations.
This is a big question. It occupied the Commonwealth Prime Ministers to a great extent at their meeting. It occupied to a great extent the meetings of OECD and the

June 17, 1975
Business of Supply
International Energy Agency recently. The big question is: How are the industrialized or developed countries going to respond to what has been described by the developing countries, or the Third World, as the new economic order which they wish to create?
If the hon. member for York West, who spoke about the United Nations, wants my opinion as to what confidence I have in the future of the United Nations, I would simply say that the United Nations at present is more deeply influenced by this question than by any other single global issue, unless it be the conflict in the Middle East. If we want to continue constructive work at the United Nations, then the industrialized countries will have to enter into a dialogue with the developing countries on this very question.
We as a government have not accepted without reservation the analysis of the world economy which has almost become the conventional wisdom in the Third World. Neither have we accepted all of the demands and remedies put forward by developing countries, some of which, in our view, would be detrimental to international development in the long run. However, the Canadian attitude toward some rearrangement of the world economy to accelerate the economic and social transformation of the Third World has been generally sympathetic, and I hope will continue to be forthcoming.
There are some tough questions that have to be faced. The interdepartmental committee, and now the standing committee of this House, that will be conducting the review will have to deal with such questions as commercial policy, both the ways in which we participate in international trade, and the instrumentalities of our bilateral trade with developing countries. It will have to take into account also our approach to international commodity agreements, the ways and means by which Canadian technology is made available to developing countries and the framework within which Canadian enterprise can participate in the industrialization of the Third World. I am sure that it will be easier for the government to develop policies in these areas if, in conjunction with the committee's examination, members of the House of Commons also study the question.
Members of the House must be aware that most rearrangements of the economic policies which would be of benefit to developing countries will also involve some cost to the Canadian economy and the Canadian people. The question really is what costs would be considered appropriate and bearable by Canadians. I leave this question on that point. Because if we do seriously want to participate in this dialogue we have to give here and there and be ready to make some compromises and sacrifices so as to make this whole dialogue meaningful.
The hon. member for St. Paul's who spoke about the United Nations should be reassured that the dialogue is beginning, and that the special session of the United Nations General Assembly to be convened in September will give us the first real opportunity to begin that dialogue in a meaningful way. At the last general assembly it was apparent to me that while the so-called automatic majority was able to carry resolutions, and the majority did carry resolutions on the subject of the new economic order. The resolutions were not concurred in by the

minority made up of industrial countries, which, if the resolutions were to get anywhere, would in the long run have to bring about their implementation.
My hon. friend has spoken about the European conference on security and co-operation, and I am also pleased that he has focused attention on this particular subject matter. He has asked some specific questions and I am able to tell him that, since the end of May there has been a perceptible quickening in the pace of the conference, and the goal of concluding at least the negotiation stage by the end of July now seems realistic. We, as a country, have been particularly interested in making progress on the so-called "basket three" which includes a range of humanitarian questions, the reunification of families and so on. In any event, the progress has been encouraging and the human contacts and education sub-committees have almost finished their work. That is the situation at the present time. The prospects for the conference seem very good and we are hopeful that progress will continue and that there will be a balance of substantial result to this important phase of the process of detente.
The hon. member for Greenwood also raised the question of whether we intended to participate in any way in the reconstruction of Indo-China. I am happy to advise my hon. friend that I have approved just recently, within the last day or so, the contribution of $1 million to the international Red Cross, which will use that money for humanitarian purposes. In addition to that, the balance of $9 million in the form of $4 million untied grants and $5 million in food aid will be approved when the United Nations appeal is launched. We will provide this money for humanitarian reconstruction purposes under the aegis of international organizations.
On the question of the Palestinian Liberation Organization and its possible attendance at the United Nations conference in Toronto this fall, as has been stated by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration and by the Acting Prime Minister, the President of the Privy Council, this is a complicated and difficult question. Canada is not the invitee to this conference. The inviting party is the United Nations itself. When Canada undertook, sought indeed, to host this conference, it undertook the obligation of receiving those invited by the United Nations.
The question of the admissibility of any particular individuals is still a matter to be decided, but I want to assure my hon. friend, whom I thank for his words of sympathy at the beginning of his speech, that international terrorists and international terrorism is as abhorrent to me as it is to him. If he wants to refresh his memory on the speeches made at the General Assembly of the United Nations last fall, I think he will find that the strongest denunciation made against international terrorism and terrorists was made by myself when I spoke at that assembly.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I have listened with interest to the response of the minister to the concerns expressed by a number of members today about the dangers involved in nuclear proliferation, for it is a subject of vital concern not only to Canadians but to every person in this global village.
Our party has expressed its reservations on many occasions about the effectiveness of the government's safeguards regarding the export of nuclear materials and technology. In listening to the minister tonight and, indeed, in listening to the Prime Minister on past occasions, trying to reassure the House and the people of Canada that the government's safeguards program announced in December 1974 was sufficiently stringent to offset the dangers in the export of nuclear technology, I am reminded of the statement of Hannes Alfven, the 1970 Nobel Laureate in physics, when he said:
Fission energy advocates claim to have taken all reasonable precautions to eliminate risks-This may very well be true, but it is irrelevant. If a problem is too difficult to solve, one cannot claim that it is solved by referring to all the efforts to solve it.
The Leader of the Opposition in calling for a moratorium on the export of nuclear reactors until stricter controls have been agreed to by the six exporting nations expressed for all of us the concerns about Canada's role in increasing the danger of proliferation of nuclear power for military purposes, and, regardless of all the minister's protestations to the contrary, it does not seem to me that we have been reassured on this subject tonight. It was not until last December that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources announced we would seek safeguards, but he made no mention at that time of the non-proliferation treaty, and he did not specify how complete the inspections which would be required would be.
In that statement of December 20, 1974, regarding the safeguards in respect of the sale abroad of Canadian nuclear technology, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources referred only peripherally to his earlier guidelines on uranium enrichment. While there have been many comments today about the fact that the safeguard statement was inadequate and ineffective, the government has been woefully silent as to a policy regarding the processing and export of enriched uranium, and this at a time when the processing of enriched uranium, a highly fissionable substance, a substance which cannot be used in Canada and which if processed can only be used for export, is under serious consideration in this country.
We find that uranium can be enriched from about 2 per cent up to 92 per cent. The purpose of enriching it slightly is to make it useful as a fuel for light-water nuclear reactors of the type used to supply power in the United States and many other parts of the world. When enriched above 20 per cent, however, uranium becomes a substitute for plutonium as the key component of a nuclear bomb and an extremely dangerous substance both to the environment and to human beings that come into contact with it. It is safe to say that any country with nuclear ambitions prefers the acquisition of enrichment facilities, for example, of enriched uranium with its easier adaptability to that of the CANDU reactor which uses natural uranium. Reprocessing and enrichment plants are the most logical
Business of Supply
target for attempts to divert fissionable fuels either by a government bent on joining the nuclear club or by terrorist factions. For this reason the United States government has discouraged U.S. companies from exporting reprocessing technology and has only recently been willing to share enrichment technology, and then under only closely controlled circumstances.
Germany, on the other hand, proposes to provide to Brazil the technology for a fuel fabrication plant, a chemical reprocessing plant for extracting plutonium from spent fuel and a uranium enrichment plant for concentrating the fissionable isotope uranium 235. The last two items in the German package worry arms control analysts more than anything else. And one has to ask how Brazil, given this access to enriched uranium and all the dangers inherent in its possession, will view the acquisition of a CANDU reactor by Argentina.
Concern has been expressed here today, and rightly so, about the export of our CANDU reactors to countries with little or no record of political stability. But equally, perhaps more, dangerous is the contemplation of the sale of a far more facile fissionable substance, enriched uranium, to countries which will not sign the non-proliferation treaty.
I would like to refer to the comments by my colleague, the member for Regina East, when in replying to the minister's statement on safeguards on December 20, 1974, he made this reference to enriched uranium as recorded at page 2430 of Hansard:
The reference in the minister's statement today to the policy guidelines on uranium enrichment announced August 1, 1973 is totally inadequate to meet this situation. The minister's failure to detail specifically the safeguards to be applied to the export of enriched uranium leads to the conclusion that Canada should not involve itself in the export of enriched uranium until specific policies to meet the situation have been worked out and have received the approval of parliament. That, we submit, should be the government's position. But if it is not, and if the government is prepared to go ahead and export enriched uranium from the James Bay area to a country like France-and we have heard this discussed-then it is time the Canadian people were told far more about this project than they have to date.
As the minister knows, the more uranium is enriched, the more easily it is converted into nuclear explosive. Fully enriched uranium is as dangerous and fissile as plutonium itself, the key component of a nuclear bomb. Are we going to export such a substance to a country like France which has an active program of nuclear testing and has never signed the non-proliferation treaty? In 1965, the then prime minister, Mr. Pearson, specifically refused to export natural uranium to France. How much more important is it today not to export a far more dangerous form of enriched uranium to that country without absolutely stringent guarantees that it will in no way facilitate or free up their own resources for their military program?
That is the statement that has never been answered in this House. These are the questions which were raised last December and never replied to. Neither the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources nor the Prime Minister, in response to many questions in this House, have taken the opportunity to outline clearly and succinctly the government position with regard to the export of enriched uranium. Yet such an undertaking which is being seriously considered would involve loss of scarce energy resources and diversion of our badly needed economic resources.
But these pale in comparison when viewed in the perspective of yet another potential nuclear substance,

June 17, 1975
Business of Supply
enriched uranium, being exported by Canada to countries over which we would have no control concerning the ultimate use of that substance whether for peaceful or military purposes. Because of the concern of hundreds of thousands of Canadians about this project I would urge the minister of make clear the government's position on enriched uranium. I would urge him to reassure the House and the country that we will not be entering into another potential means of nuclear proliferation.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, I was most delighted to hear the minister refer to his interest in helping mankind. That was the reason we got into this business of selling CANDU reactors. The idea was to help Third World countries develop alternate sources of energy rather than use their few precious reserves to buy oil. That has always struck me as rather strange. Sometimes I wonder about the kind of roles we play and the kind of things we say in this House and in bodies such as the United Nations when I see the way in which we perform.
I should like to leave the minister with a question which I hope at some time in this debate he will be good enough to answer. He is very interested in helping mankind in the technological field. That is very admirable, but we cannot escape the fact that our record with regard to Southwest Africa, and specifically Namibia, is not one of which we should be proud. The United Nations has taken a very firm position with regard to South Africa turning over Namibia to Namibians. There is the trusteeship of the United Nations which we support, and we want to help Third World countries develop. We want to help Namibia.
However, we have the most despicable situation in which South Africa has refused to hand over the resources of Namibia to the trusteeship of the United Nations. Canada supported that position by its very admirable conduct at the United nations and by the speeches of our representatives, but now can we put some action to those words? One of the ways to do so would be to come to grips with the situation in respect of the Falconbridge Nickel Mines. Falconbridge Nickel Mines is one of Canada's most powerful multinational corporations. Indeed, it is not a Canadian multinational corporation because it is owned by a very wealthy foreign company. However, it operates out of Canada using Canada as its home base. Falconbridge operates in Namibia. It uses native workers. It does not develop the skills of those workers so that in the future they would be able to take over the operation of Falconbridge. These people are used as indentured workers. They are returned to their compounds after they have been used.
Falconbridge's record is clear to the world, and the minister is well aware of it. And yet, Falconbridge in Namibia is permitted to write-off from their federal income tax in Canada whatever royalties or taxes they pay to the South African government. I do not ask the minister to interfere in the internal operations of South Africa with regard to Falconbridge, but surely if we are concerned about the developing countries we have a responsibility to say to Falconbridge, "Henceforth you will not be permitted to write-off the taxes and royalties or any other payments to the South African government for the operation

on Namibian lands". That is action, Madam Chairman, not pussyfooting around saying we cannot interfere in the internal workings of a country. Canada is before the world a partner in Falconbridge's rip-off of the Namibian people, of the South West Africans. Surely, when we talk about some kind of relevance in the developing world, and when we make all our great speeches on helping these countries develop, we must come to grips with that problem. The minister must answer why it is we cannot tell Falconbridge in Namibia that they are not permitted to write-off, under section 6 of the Income Tax Act, any royalties or taxes paid to the South African government.
The second question I would like to ask concerns a matter that is of great interest to me. We are in the process of selling a CANDU reactor to Argentina. I could understand it if Argentina were a struggling third world country and we tried to help them develop their technology for alternate sources of energy, but in light of what has been taking place in Argentina we know the situation there is not stable. The situation there is pretty volatile, with extreme right wing elements and extreme left wing elements knocking each other off. Every night we hear that four people were killed there and three people were killed in another place. An extremely volatile political situation exists there at present. And what are we doing? We are putting into the hands of Isabel Peron the means by which in the future, whoever takes over that government, would say to Canada, "Get out, you have no jurisdiction here".
Madam Chairman, these are questions that create a great doubt in my mind. When we say we are so concerned about helping mankind, are we really trying to help mankind or are we trying to do what the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce said in the discussion on Bill C-9 earlier this year in the finance committee? He said, let us not forget that when selling these CANDU reactors we have to make bucks for Canada. That is what the name of the game is, it is making bucks. If we can sell a CANDU reactor for $600 million, by George, we will even help finance it. The name of the game is making bucks.
What I really wanted to say is that we should take a look at the whole situation of aid to see how Canada deals with Third World developing countries in providing aid. In the past few years, there have been a variety of scandals concerning CIDA's aid program reported in the press: money expended for railroads that do not exist, sewer systems that do not work, and so on. Such scandals provide the media with tomorrow's story, but such administrative oversights prevent us from understanding why the gap between rich and poor is growing. What needs.to be questioned is the whole structure, the organization and the ideology upon which the present Canadian aid program has been built. In fact, the present aid programs are designed quite consciously to prevent the less developed countries from developing self-reliant socio-economic societies. But what can we expect from a country which is itself dominated by the United States? Of course, we need to scrutinize CIDA and Canadian participation in various international banks as well as the International Monetary Fund, of which the Minister of Finance is currently the chairman.
The bulk of Canadian aid, for example, is channelled through the bilateral division of CIDA. Although there is
June 17, 1975

some possibility of change, bilateral funds are tied to the purchase of Canadian goods to the tune of at least 80 per cent. Bilateral aid accounts for about 60 per cent to 70 per cent of CIDA's budget, multilateral aid accounts for another 20 per cent to 30 per cent, and the non-governmental organization division accounts for another 10 per cent. Yet CIDA quite consciously overpublicizes the non-governmental organization division, that is the international charities and the churches, no doubt to give CIDA-type aid a good name.
The question at issue is the effect of the kind of aid that Canada among others in the west has been supplying to the Third World: what we find is that the effect of aid over the past 20 years has been to tie the Third World countries into the west's economic system so tightly that in general the non-communist Third World finds itself in a progressively deteriorating position.
The effects of inflation have, of course, been devastating, but inflation is not a new thing to many Third World countries. In the mid-sixties Brazil, for example, was experiencing inflation rates of 45 per cent to 60 per cent a year. In fact the only hope in the present international economic crisis is that it may provide real opportunities for Third World countries to develop self-reliance. In the period between 1950 to the end of 1973, we find that prices for Canadian exports such as zinc ore increased 350 per cent; nickel, 250 per cent; lumber, 215 per cent; wheat, 160 per cent; whereas the export price increase of such Third World commodities as bauxite is only 76 per cent. Even sugar increased only 73.4 per cent; coffee only 44.2 per cent and tea decreased 24.8 per cent.
Moreover, when you look at the percentage change in real purchasing power in terms of manufactured goods, we find in every one of these cases but bauxite a real decline in purchasing power. The present economic crisis has forced the west to at least pay attention to the ridiculous situation where Third World countries which had been receiving so-called aid found that the debt service as a percentage of gross lending ranged from 40 per cent to 87 per cent in 1967. How has this situation arisen?
The international monetary and banking institutions and their operating philosophies developed in the period after World War II and are a direct consequence of the depression. In essence, they were attempts to gain back for large capitalist trading nations economic supremacy in the non-western world, that is control of the resources and markets. The depression dealt a fatal blow to the gold standard. After the war, the major trading nations, especially the U.S. which just prior to the depression had begun to challenge the U.K. for domination of world trade, tried to devise institutions which would reconcile bo*h the exchange rate stability of the gold standard and the insistence of nation states on managing their own economies so as to minimize the possibilities of depression and unemployment, that is to internationalize Keynesian economics. The system was fashioned at Bretton-Woods in 1944; it was to be enforced by the IMF and was called the par value system of fixed but adjustable exchange rates.
The ideology of the IMF and its sister institution, the World Bank, is one of economic liberalism. The dominant force was and still is the U.S.-Canada, as in the case of the duplicity that led to the fall of Allende, just tags along,
Business of Supply
picking up a trade crumb here and an export dollar there. The IMF's philosophy calls for the widest possible freedom of play for market forces and frowns on any kind of government intervention such as price subsidies, rationing, protection of domestic industries. These are seen as distortions of the free market relations.
Consider some of the major features of the IMF's so-called stabilization program: First, abolition or liberalization of foreign exchange and import controls; second, domestic anti-inflationary programs, including: (a) control of government deficit; curbs on spending; increases in taxes and in prices charged by public enterprises; abolition of consumer subsidies; (b) control of wage rises, so far as is within the government's power; (c) dismantling of price controls; third, greater hospitality to foreign investment. Does that sound familiar, Madam Chairman?
The IMF policy of development, along with that of the various international banks, supports the internationalizing of Third World economies. Because local capital is used to finance the projects of international corporations such as Falconbridge, many Third World countries find it difficult, given cash shortages, to develop local substitutes to western imports. This leads to a circular process of dependency. An example of such dependency can be seen in the case of Chile, which was highly dependent upon food imports. Yet Chile has a potential agricultural productivity comparable to that of California. Canada helped prevent Chile from renegotiating loans which had been taken on by the previous administration. The distortions such economic dependencies cause prevent the development of industries which would appear to be natural to many areas of the Third World.
An example of what internationalization does for a Third World country could be seen in Mozambique prior to its liberation. Thousands of acres of fertile land were used to grow coffee for export, yet people in these areas were suffering from malnutrition. Moreover, a variant of this theme was put forward by agribusiness at the food conference. The large agribusiness corporations assured the conference that they could supply the needs of the Third World. Many of the products they can supply will, of course, be supplied from the west and hence use up valuable foreign exchange and prevent the development of locally-produced import substitutes. Moreover, to pay for these imports, countries must build up foreign reserves. To do this they must encourage the growth of cash crops and other crude exports, in many cases at the expense of feeding their populations. Yet even after making the sacrifice of malnutrition, export earnings never seem to match the value of western imports needed to run the kind of economy of which such countries as Canada approve.
If this were not enough, two other but related factors exacerbate the problems of the Third World. First, increasing foreign ownership by multinational corporations goes hand in hand with the liberalization of imports and exchange controls. Second, the role aid plays in Third World economies is clearly aimed at maintaining Third World dependency. The economic advice given western financial institutions, upon whose boards Canada sits, is quite clearly deflationary in nature. Liberalization of exchange and import controls means simply the disman-
6864

June 17, 1975
Business of Supply
tling of devices which were originally instituted to save foreign exchange. Such controls allow local leaders to decide what are necessities and what are luxuries. In fact, this requirement is a basic objective of the IMF. It results inevitably in an increased shortage of these funds in Third World countries.
World financial institutions, along with the Canadian government, try to promote the international flow of trade and investment and oppose modes of development which restrict this flow. Liberalization of trade and foreign investment, combined with the deflationary aspects of the IMF's rules, benefit the foreign-owned firms which are dependent on foreign imports imported from other branches of the same multinational corporations.
If, for example, foreign exchange for imports were severely controlled, that is, in order to encourage the development of local substitutes, then foreign-owned factories might have to cut down their production or seek local substitutes. Most multinational corporations prefer intracorporate trade because they are then free to set the prices and hence can transfer the profits from one country to another in the guise of payments for imports.
The recessionary conditions which trade liberalization causes lead to a situation where many Third World companies must either curtail operations and lay off workers or actually cease operating, that is, through bankruptcy. In other words, they become ripe for takeover by foreign companies at bargain basement prices. Although the means are different in Canada, the pattern of takeover is the same. And, as in Canada, these corporations usually finance takeovers by borrowing from local banks. Because of their size and wealth, local banks are assured that their money is safe, and hence prefer to lend money to multinationals rather than to .local companies. A trade liberalization program leads to foreign takeovers, the inability to develop local substitutes to foreign imports and shortages of foreign exchange. The latter is, of course, crucial. Without this, payments for the liberalized trade policies cannot be met. Enter foreign aid.
In fact, foreign aid is not a very accurate term. It conjures up the notion of gifts to Third World countries. The term "aid", as it has developed since World War II, means any international financial transaction, all the way from an outright grant to a loan at just below the going commercial interest'rates. The loans sections of aid programs make up the largest percentage of CIDA's bilateral and multilateral aid programs. The purpose of aid, remember, is to support development which leads to the promotion of international flow of trade and investment. Aid, in fact, is seen by IMF, international banks and aid agencies such as CIDA as a means for balancing the budgets of underveloped economies.
For example, an article from Finance and Development, an IMF publication, states the following:
For, unlike the post-war aid received by European countries, aid to developing countries constitutes a continuous source of financing. In general, therefore, the recipient countries are not expected to adjust their balance of payments to do without the aid as were the European countries during the immediate post-war period.
Foreign debt then becomes the sequel to foreign aid. If market forces are allowed free play, then all manner of imports may be brought into a country without any rela-
tionship to the actual needs of that country. Some Third World countries have experimented with multiple exchange rates, that is, one rate would be used for needed items and a higher one for luxury items. Such a system acts in the same way as a tax subsidy does. Such policies obviously interfere with trade, and hence are anathema to so-called free enterprise countries such as Canada. What is forgotten, however, is that most of these funds must be paid back at a later date. The importance of aid and foreign investment depends upon the degree of development a country has attained. The more developed, the more important foreign investment becomes, and vice versa.
Typically, then, aid is given for the purpose of financing such liberalized import policies, to pay for Canadian-tied aid. Such a policy not only builds up an ever-increasing debt, but also restricts the ability of the country to use its foreign reserves to import only the goods and services it actually needs and to develop locally-produced import substitutes.
A final consequence of this economic system which has developed, and of which foreign aid, as presently constituted, is an integral part, is the tendency for many Third World governments to suffer the consequences of rightist military coups. Much space is usually devoted to explain that dictatorships are the result of the democratic unpreparedness of many Third World countries, but such simplistic theories ignore the reality of world power.

subtopic: EFFECT OF BILINGUAL POLICY ON TEMPORARY EMPLOYEES

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: EFFECT OF BILINGUAL POLICY ON TEMPORARY EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise tonight to raise a matter which I raised when the estimates of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) were before the House on May 9. That was the problem created in the Public Service of this country with respect to the implementation of the policy of bilingualism as it affects term or casual employees. This is a very important question and has affected a great number of public servants. At that time I said to the President of the Treasury Board that I felt the policy which had been enunciated just a day or so before was discriminatory and unfair to unilingual Canadians.
I said that on the basis that the policy as announced indicated that before any person could be appointed as a casual employee to a position designated bilingual in the Public Service of Canada, that person had to be bilingual at the outset. No language training is provided for term employees. There are a number of term employees who wish that language training could be provided, but apparently that is not the case. Given the failure of language training and given this new rule of implementation that those employees must be bilingual at the outset, it comes to my attention that a large number of Canadians through an accident of birth and geography, are denied casual or term employment in the Public Service.
I raise this grievance because I truly believe it is discriminatory. I raise this grievance because I want the government to consider the inequity of this position. I raise this grievance because in the Department of National Revenue approximately 2,000 casual employees are affected by this policy. In so far as they are concerned, they have had some relief but I emphasize the quote "some" because the evil day has merely been put off for them until some event, perhaps two or three years distant takes place. This applies to many other departments which do not even have the benefit of that paltry order, and I would respectfully suggest that it is to that problem the attention of the government ought to be addressed.
I hesitated to raise this grievance, but it has been submitted to me and many other members by petition. I hope that members on both sides of the House will consider the position of persons who, by the accident of birth, geography and environment, cannot now qualify even as a term or casual employee in the public service of their country.
I raised this matter before and I feel compelled to raise it again because all parties supported the principles of the Official Languages Act. In so far as this small group of Canadians is concerned-a group that will probably grow-I cannot believe that it was ever meant they would be discriminated against in terms of service with the government on a casual basis. I hope that, as a result of raising this matter, there will be some indication that it will be reviewed by the President of the Treasury Board. I believe it is important.
There is a great danger in this whole matter of improper implementation-not wrong principle but improper implementation. I think it is important to the fabric of our country that we jealously guard the propriety of the implementation of this very important policy which is supported in principle by all parties. The difficulty does not lie with the policy, but with its practical implementa-

June 17, 1975
Grievance
tion in the public service. I earnestly hope that the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) will consider this situation and consult the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) about it, with a view to seeing that persons casually employed by the public service will not be denied the right to employment in the public service of their own country. I am concerned about that aspect.
Let me repeat my request. I ask the President of the Treasury Board to consult with his colleagues to see whether this inequity-potential for some and real for others-cannot be corrected. Surely, the inequitable order could be revoked as easily as it was put through in the first place. Surely, we can help those who wish to work for the public service of this country in that way.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre De Bane (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs

speechtext:
On the same subject, Madam Speaker, I think the hon. member who spoke before me should explain that the French-speaking community still has the main grievances. Indeed, when one looks at positions in the federal public service, one realizes that the great majority have been classified as English unilingual, and in a far greater proportion than that of the anglophone population, and conversely, when it comes to Francophones who represent more than or almost 30 per cent of the Canadian population, the percentage of positions in the public service that have been designated as French unilingual is not 30 per cent.
I would also like to remind the hon. member that according to the statistics submitted by the Public Service Commission for a number of years, Francophones are underrepresented in the federal public service, at all levels, in all departments and at every level in every department. And when the hon. member talks about discrimination, I would like to remind him that today the working language in most departments, agencies and institutions of the federal government is still English and English exclusively, and if there is a group against which the current policy of the government discriminates, it is Francophones. I quite agree with the hon. member that one must not look to the past.

We should not look to the past; we should look to the future. I was happy to hear the hon. member agree to the principle on which the policy is based. It is encouraging to note that most members of this House support the policy. It can be expressed in another way. It is a policy for national unity. For me, bilingualism is one means of achieving and strengthening national unity; it is a means of making sure that all Canadians feel at home in Canada, that they all feel the central government represents them, that the whole country is theirs, and that they need not retreat to one province.
We should examine the program from all aspects. Usually, after people have been hired for temporary employment in the public service, they end up obtaining permanent jobs in the public service. When they enter the competition, the knowledge and experience they gained on the job while working temporarily stands them in good stead; so the odds of their getting the job are high.


I think, Madam Speaker, that in the main the implementation of that policy may cause problems but in my opinion we must admit that altogether it is the French-speaking community which is mainly entitled to complain. As a matter of fact, the report of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism as well as the annual reports of the Commissioner of Official Languages, who incidentally is doing a marvellous job, show abundantly that it is indeed against the French-speaking community that the current policy discriminates.

subtopic: EFFECT OF BILINGUAL POLICY ON TEMPORARY EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member raised a point which is of concern in the national capital region. I believe it relates to term and temporary employees in supervisory positions. Those who are appointed to term or temporary supervisory positions are, according to a recent Treasury Board interpretation, required to be bilingual. The employees of whom the hon. member spoke, supervisory employees of the Department of National Revenue who have been, in many cases, called back year after year in a temporary supervisory capacity to do work connected with the preparation of income tax returns, constitute a special case. This matter was brought to the attention of the minister and Treasury Board. As the hon. member who raised the grievance pointed out, an order was issued to exclude those temporary employees from the operation of the policy. I have taken this matter up with the President of the Treasury Board and other public officials and there is a review taking place in the national capital region involving other employees who are in similar positions.
One of the inequities of the situation I suggest is this: those employees are not given priority for language training. They will not be accepted for language training although in many cases they have come back every year for the past 15 or 20 years to do the same kind of work. They have taken a temporary appointment which does not last the whole year and does not lead to permanent employment in the department. Because there is a lack of facilities for language training in the language school and because these employees constitute a special case, Treasury Board is currently reviewing the matter. I am sure the hon. member will wait, as will others representing the national capital region, for modifications in policy and developments which will deal with this special situation.

subtopic: NATIONAL PARKS-ENTRANCE FEES-COMPLAINTS FROM RADIUM AND INVERMERE REGARDING REDUCED BUSINESS REVENUE-HONOUR SYSTEM FOR THROUGH TRAFFIC
NATIONAL PARKS-ENTRANCE FEES-COMPLAINTS FROM RADIUM AND INVERMERE REGARDING REDUCED BUSINESS REVENUE-HONOUR SYSTEM FOR THROUGH TRAFFIC
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, a few days ago I asked the minister responsible for our national parks a question. It was prompted by representations made by people living in the towns and villages of my constituency and concerned the new fee schedule which has been posted for the national parks. Of course, this question had been raised indirectly a little while before I asked it; it was raised in the grievance period, following committee of supply proceedings similar to those of today.
At that time the minister replied by saying that the new policy is designed to have the users pay for the parks; he quoted a figure. As I recall, he said that 5 per cent of all Canadians used the parks. That figure may sound good; it may sound plausible, but if one examines it one will see it is fallacious, because there are no large national parks close to the large population centres of Ontario and Quebec. On the other hand, in British Columbia, some national parks straddle the Trans-Canada highway and I suggest that park users in British Columbia constitute a far larger proportion of the population than 5 per cent, a proportion larger probably than that of any province except Alberta, which is in the same position as British Columbia. Therefore, some of the problems in British Columbia and Alberta are different from those in the rest of the country.
The people who write to me are particularly concerned about the complicated and impractical fee schedule. I do not know what will happen when the summer traffic of July and August hits the national parks gates of Alberta and British Columbia, especially the gates of parks which straddle the Trans-Canada highway. Every car which approaches the park gate will be confronted with six choices, six options, and the people in the car will need to decide, almost instantaneously which of the six choices to make. They must decide whether to go right through or whether to stay one, two, three, four or five days and get a ticket for all national parks for the whole year. It will not be easy to sort out that traffic. I suspect there will be trouble at the gates. There will be increased trouble when the summer flow of traffic builds up. I understand the honour system has already been abandoned. When it was suggested that it would be used, I did not feel it would last a week, I gather it hardly lasted that long.
The other thing about it is that it could well be disastrous to established businesses inside the parks. These people are not consulted when the rules of the game are changed significantly for them. I have received representations, which I have sent to the minister, which indicate that business has dropped off very sharply. I feel the move was made without a clear appreciation of the community nature some of the businesses inside the park have for towns that are a considerable distance outside the park in British Columbia. Meetings of the Invermere-Windermere chamber of commerce are frequently held at the lodge at Radium, inside the park. It serves the role of a community gathering place. With the new fee schedule, every time a person attends each of perhaps five meetings, there is an
Adjournment Debate
extra charge that was not there previously because the definition of a user of park facilities is very narrow. If a meeting of the chamber of commerce is held inside the park, those people who would normally simply attend would now become users of a park facility and liable to the extra fee.
I have had representations from the Invermere-Winder-mere chamber of commerce suggesting that if the fee had to be increased, and realizing the inflationary pressures, it would have been far better to set it at a straight $5. That would not have necessitated the complicated policing that will be necessary. It would have saved the confusion at the gates and would probably not have had as detrimental an effect on those businesses that are established in the park.
The minister suggested he will try this for a year. I suggest that some of the businesses within the national park could be in considerable trouble if there is no relief and no change. The traffic on the Trans-Canada highway will be badly snarled if there is no provision to review the whole situation before a year.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Iona Campagnolo (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: NATIONAL PARKS-ENTRANCE FEES-COMPLAINTS FROM RADIUM AND INVERMERE REGARDING REDUCED BUSINESS REVENUE-HONOUR SYSTEM FOR THROUGH TRAFFIC
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the minister has to date received only one letter from the Radium-Windermere area of British Columbia concerning alleged decline of business in an operation in Kootenay National Park. This will be answered in the next few days.
The new schedule of park fees was introduced as of April 1. The combined visitation to the park in 1975 for April-May has been below the recorded visitation in 1974 for the same period. Park officers indicate, however, that much of this has been due to the Easter holiday occurring in March this year and because of poor weather during both months.
Park officers indicate that operation of the entranceway at Kootenay National Park is posing no special problems as a result of the new fee schedule. This is particularly so now that through traffic on the Banff-Windermere highway, which has free passage, is identified by through passes which are temporarily affixed to vehicles.
The intention, of course, is to collect a park fee only from those people who intend to stop and use the park and the facilities in it. Though Kootenay park has posed no special problems, it can be said that fees application in all national parks will be reviewed after the summer season to endeavour to correct any anomalies that may be identified during the main operating season.
I should like to assure the hon. member for Okanagan-Kootenay (Mr. Johnston), as a person who has enjoyed swimming in Aquacourt at Radium and the various facilities in that area, that confusions and troubles at the gate are not our goal. We seek better parks through public participation, by ordinary people making their acceptable contributions to that park's upgrading program by their monetary contribution when they are in the park.

subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-POSSIBILITY OF TASK FORCE TO STUDY WAGE POLICY IN ATLANTIC REGION
REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-POSSIBILITY OF TASK FORCE TO STUDY WAGE POLICY IN ATLANTIC REGION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the question that I raised in the House

June 17, 1975
Adjournment Debate
yesterday requesting an in-depth study of the federal wage policy as it affects all federal workers in the Atlantic region seems to me, and to most members from that area, a reasonable request. In fact, given the vague and ambiguous answers offered by the minister in charge of DREE, as well as the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien), as a rationale for the present policy, we feel that it is imperative to get such a study.
We are fed up with being reminded by the President of the Treasury Board that "for a number of occupational groups in the public service, a regional approach to rates of pay has been in effect for many years". The fact that a wage policy is an old one is not sufficient for it to be considered a valid or equitable one. We are also tired of being told, as the DREE minister told me in May, 1975 in hearings before the Standing Committee on Regional Economic Expansion, that "it is not just the federal government that has regional rates".
I would remind the minister that when the present minister of external affairs took over the labour portfolio, one of the first things he did was to raise the federal minimum wage above that then granted by provincial jurisdictions because, as he said then, the federal government has to give leadership in this field. Giving leadership when it comes to justice for blue collar workers and others in the Atlantic region seems to be the last thing on the minds of the treasury board decision-makers.
The facts are these, Madam Speaker. Fact No. 1-Disparity exists in wages paid to federal employees in different regions of Canada. Fact No. 2-The Department of Regional Economic Expansion was set up in 1969 to help close the income gap that exists between different regions of Canada. Fact No. 3-Many federally employed public servants in Atlantic Canada receive less, indeed much less, than do their counterparts in other regions. Fact No. 4- These federal wage disparities exist even though federal income taxes are paid on an equal basis in all regions of Canada. Fact No. 5-It takes the same effort, mental and physical, to do the same job within the federal service wherever the worker is employed in Canada. Fact No. 6- The present high cost of living is, if anything, higher in the Atlantic region. Fact No. 7-The recent increase in pay of members of parliament was the same all across Canada, on the basis of equal pay for equal work. Fact No. 8-The recent increase in judges' pay was the same all across Canada.
However, when it comes to blue collar jobs in the federal sector of the Atlantic region, the equal pay for equal work principle goes out the window. There is an annual difference of some $4,306 a year for a certain class of electrician in the federal government service if that person works in Vancouver rather than Sydney or Halifax, Nova Scotia. Federal government carpenters get $6.42 in Toronto and $5.23 in Halifax and Moncton. There is rank discrimination when we consider that the federal government as an employer pays an unskilled labourer $4.80 in Vancouver but only $3.82 in New Brunswick. Hospital workers, janitors, general labour and tradesmen and many other categories of people are also affected in a similar manner.
In an answer given in May, 1975 to the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) concerning the

total annual cost of regional rate elimination for all government employees, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) estimated that it would cost about $79 million. If we accept that figure as fairly accurate, then, of course, it would be reduced by the amount of all forms of taxes, direct and indirect, which are paid to all levels of government.
The multiplier effect of such an expenditure, even correcting for losses from such an income stream through personal savings, taxes and buying of imported goods, would have a significant effect on the growth of income in the Atlantic region. In any case, all we are requesting is an in-depth, comprehensive and detailed study of this federal wage policy. What we are getting as answers to our concerns are glib general rationalizations which are traditionally vague. The time is overdue for such an objective study, because it should be clear to everybody that the present policy promotes jealousy and regional disparity, and does nothing for the unity of this country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joseph-Philippe Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-POSSIBILITY OF TASK FORCE TO STUDY WAGE POLICY IN ATLANTIC REGION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member has outlined numerous reasons why he would like to see an additional appraisal or study of the present wage policy of the federal government. He suggests that this study should concern itself, and I would like to quote him, "as it affects all federal workers in the Atlantic region".
The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) discussed with hon. members in the standing committee the efforts which DREE and other federal departments are undertaking to lessen income disparities across Canada. He also referred to the practical problems of coming to grips with the application of so-called national pay scales, which include important implications not only for the federal government but also for other levels of government as well as the private sector and unions.
I can go no further this evening than to reassure the hon. member, as the minister has done, that the government is very much aware of the need to lessen income disparities across the country. Numerous departments, including DREE and manpower, are involved in this fight, and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) has indicated that his officers are keeping abreast of changing circumstances within the public service.

subtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-LACK OF NATIVES IN SENIOR POSITIONS IN DEPARTMENT-GOVERNMENT ACTION
INDIAN AFFAIRS-LACK OF NATIVES IN SENIOR POSITIONS IN DEPARTMENT-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise tonight to deal with a question I asked the minister with reference to the number of Indian people who hold decision-making positions in the higher echelons within his department. The history of our country is not a proud one. It is not a history which is honourable. We have not treated our first Canadians in an honourable way or in a way in which I, as a Canadian, can look at with any amount of pride. As a matter of fact, it is a history that has blackened our nation.
Our policies hitherto have been steeped in ethno-cen-tricity and served white superiority. Our history is a
June 17, 1975

dismal record of two peoples in co-habitation in this country. I have a vision of the day when our Indian people will walk with us side by side with a pride their forefathers once had, but that will not be accomplished by an attitude on the part of the department that asks: What can we do for them? No, it will be accomplished by a department that allows the native people to do for themselves.
By the minister's own admission, his department has made mistakes. I quote from Hansard of June 12 at page 6695 where the minister is reported as having said:
Certainly there will be mistakes made. Lord knows, we have made more than our share.
Such true words come right from the minister himself. He goes on to state, as reported in the same page of Hansard:
We are quite prepared, with proper guidelines, to turn over to the Indian people as much responsibility for their affairs as possible. As far as I am concerned, that is a fundamental cornerstone of our policy, whether it is the management of funds or running the various other aspects that apply directly to their lives. We feel strongly that that should be the thrust.
Madam Speaker, here we have a minister who says it is his desire to have the department managed to the greatest possible degree by the native Canadians, the Indian people, in line with the thought of the native people having self-determination and who then contradicts that by the most blatant examples of inaction. I speak particularly of inaction in appointing native people to the decision-making positions within his department. I should like the minister to name for me five positions in Ottawa, referred to as the higher echelon of his department, which have been filled by Indian persons. That might be too difficult for him to do, so I shall ask him to name four or three or two. I challenge the minister to name one single solitary position in the higher echelons that is filled by a native Canadian. He cannot do that because there is not one position filled by an Indian person.
On June 13, when I asked the minister when he intends to appoint to one of these hundreds of positions a native Canadian he replied, as recorded at page 6732 of Hansard for June 13:
Mr. Speaker, I have some thoughts in these areas and am currently pursuing them with my colleagues in cabinet.
The minister says he has some thoughts in these areas. I should think after 100 years of bungling and making the kinds of mistakes that have been made he should have more than thoughts. He should be able to give me some names. He should have some responsible leaders in this country administering the policies which hitherto have been anything but in line with the concept of self-determination. I believe we, the white people, are responsible for turning our reserves into ghettos of poverty. We the white people, have stripped the native people of their pride. We have made them beggars in their own land. If the minister adopted this method of appointing native people and involving them in decision-making roles this would give us an opportunity to demonstrate our faith in the ability of the Indian people to run their own affairs. It is not that they demand respect, but rather that they are worthy of it.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Iona Campagnolo (Parliamentary Secretery to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-LACK OF NATIVES IN SENIOR POSITIONS IN DEPARTMENT-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Adjournment Debate
Madam Speaker, I am pleased that the hon. member took less than his allotted time because the amount of work which has been done in this field is so great I should like, if possible, to take longer than the regular time. I shall begin by saying that in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, for example, at the end of December, 1974 there were a total of 1,188 Innuit and Indian employees. This represents approximately 13 per cent of the department's total manpower. In addition there were 362 casual or term native employees. Of the total, two native employees were in the executive category while more than 300 were in responsible positions in the administrative and foreign service, scientific and professional categories. The balance were employed in technical, administrative support and operational categories.
The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Whiteway) spoke about my minister during the last 100 years. While he is a relatively youthful man, I do not think 100 years would really do him justice. The honesty of the minister I have the honour to represent is unquestioned, and if he says he had some doubt about the efficiency of the program I think the hon. member should be honoured to receive those remarks in this House.
The employment of native people in the public service, in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, and in the private sector is a high priority that is being pursued conscientiously and vigorously by the department.

subtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-LACK OF NATIVES IN SENIOR POSITIONS IN DEPARTMENT-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: Name them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-LACK OF NATIVES IN SENIOR POSITIONS IN DEPARTMENT-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
I named 1,188. I also named two who are in executive capacities. However, the hon. member may not be interested in these facts I am attempting to give him. We recognize that native people are significantly under-represented in the labour force. We know that this is the combined result of their socio-economically disadvantaged position and the consequent inability to compete on equal terms with non-Indian workers as well as a reluctance on the part of some to move into the wage-earning economy.
The department has a large number of programs aimed at dealing with this problem both directly and indirectly. In general, the economic development activities that the Indian and Eskimo affairs and northern programs undertake through various loans and grants are aimed at generating employment opportunities for the native people. The department has a wide range of educational and vocational training programs that are designed to enable the Indian people to acquire qualifications appropriate to their participation in the labour market. I do not believe it is stretching the point to say that the largest proportion of the department's budget is directed towards improving the economic situation of the native people.
But in addition to general economic development program which create jobs for the native people, the department has various specific programs designed to come to grips with particular employment problems.
